title: 7-day microburst telemetry playback — cluster & pool occupancy
summary: Export of fine-grained GPU occupancy telemetry over the last 7 days focused on microburst events (<= 120s) that cause transient capacity pressure. This sheet is a playback for infra on-call and capacity planning to understand which clusters/pools and tenants are responsible for high-frequency short spikes.
purpose: Operational debugging and short-term capacity tuning: identify pools with noisy short tail behavior, estimate required burst headroom, and produce targeted mitigations (slice sizing, pre-warm, reservation bumps, autoscaler tuning).
annotations: gamma-02 shows the highest frequency of <=30s peak bursts during US evening window (UTC 00:00-08:00 local).
delta-01 batch pool has long-duration spikes (30-120s) tied to periodic scheduled training windows (see INFRA-2345).
dedicated-committed pool maintains high baseline but short bursts are lower duration (<10s) and correlate with tenant rollout events.
sandbox-ephemeral has noisy fragmented occupancy; many 10-40s bursts from CI jobs—low priority but high count.
key_findings: Short microbursts (<=30s) account for ~38% of observed peak events but produce 62% of short-term SLO pressure due to autoscaler reaction lag.
P95 utilization in inference-high pools exceeds 85% during burst windows on gamma clusters; headroom <10% frequently, causing queuing spikes.
Batch pool long bursts are predictable (cron-triggered) and can be mitigated with scheduled reservation windows rather than reactive autoscale.
Node-level fragmentation: several nodes show repeated high peak_short_burst_pct while avg_util_pct remains moderate -> indicates hot-tenant colocation.
charts: time-series: cluster-level p95_util_pct (1m resolution) with annotated microburst events
cdf: burst_duration_s per pool (separate lines for pools)
heatmap: nodes x hour-of-day showing peak_short_burst_pct intensity
scatter: jobs_queued vs peak_short_burst_pct colored by tenant
operational_impact_estimates: Estimated additional reserved headroom to hit 99.9% no-queue target during peak microbursts for inference-high (gamma clusters): +12% of current pool capacity (~24 GPUs across gamma-02/03)
If we instead increase autoscaler cooldown to 45s and allow transient overcommit by 8%, projected reduction in unnecessary scale-ups: ~27% (trading some queuing for fewer churn events).
Scheduling batch-window reservations for delta-01 batch-lowprio could reduce long-duration backlog by ~70% during known windows (see linked schedule).
action_items: (A1) Short term: provision +8 GPUs of burst reserve on gamma-02 for 2-week test (owner: Markus) — due 2026-08-19
(A2) Medium term: implement tenant-level soft-isolation in inference-high pool (slicing change) to avoid hot-tenant spikes (owner: Sofia) — RFC next week
(A3) Ops: add rule to autoscaler to ignore spikes shorter than 20s when current queue < 5 to avoid thrash (owner: Devon) — PR #412
(A4) Product: notify large training tenants to move heavy scheduled runs to dedicated batch windows or purchase reserved capacity (owner: Aisha)
open_questions: What fraction of microbursts are caused by internal test traffic vs customer workloads? (need tenant metadata enrichment)
Can we cheaply add a 10s smoothing window in the placement layer without impacting p50 latency?
Is it acceptable from a cost/SL tradeoff to allow small transient queueing (p99 queue length <= 2) in exchange for fewer scale cycles?
notes: This export was generated from the occupancy-query playback tool (playback-v2) using 1m sampling and the "peak_short_burst" detector configured with a 5s sliding window. Raw logs and full resolution traces are on S3 (linked in Confluence). Use this sheet for on-call review; it contains suggested mitigations but requires validation in canary and cost model analysis.
recommended_next_steps: Run the gamma-02 8-GPU reserve test for 14 days, collect p95_util and queue metrics, then reconvene with product and SRE to finalize autoscaler policy. Update RFC for tenant-slicing and include regression tests in lab harness.
